text: You're given a list of intervals. Each one has a left end and a right end, both included, and its size is right minus left plus one. You're also given a list of queries. For each query, find the size of the smallest interval that contains it. If no interval contains it, the answer is negative one. Return the answers in the same order as the queries.

Thanks. Before I dive in, I'd like to clarify a few things. Just to make sure I'm understanding this correctly — both ends are included, so the interval two to four holds two, three and four, and its size is three? And if several intervals contain the query, I only return the smallest size, not which interval it was?
Right on both. Both ends count, and you only return the size.

Okay. One thing I want to say early: each answer depends only on the query's value, not on where it sits in the list. So I'm free to answer the queries in any order I like, as long as each answer goes back to its original slot. Are there any constraints on the input size?
Up to ten to the fifth intervals and ten to the fifth queries. Every value is between one and ten to the seventh.

Got it. A size is at most ten million, so an int is enough. Let me run through the example. Example one: intervals one to four, two to four, three to six and four to four, with queries two, three, four, five. Expected three, three, one, four. Query four sits inside all four intervals, and the point interval four to four wins with size one. Query five is only inside three to six, so its answer is four.

Hmm, let me think about this for a sec. A naive approach would be to scan every interval for every query. That's ten to the fifth times ten to the fifth, about ten billion checks, which is too slow. This problem reminds me of an offline sweep line with a min-heap. Since the queries are independent, I can sort them and sweep from small to large. As the sweep moves right, an interval becomes a candidate once its left end is passed, and it stops being one once its right end falls behind. A heap ordered by size keeps the smallest candidate on top.
You order the heap by size, but you throw things out by right end. Why not just key it by the right end?

Because the answer is the smallest size, and the right end tells me nothing about size. Take intervals one to three and three to four, with query three. Both contain three. Keyed by right end, the top is one to three, so I'd answer three. But three to four has size two, which is the right answer. My first draft did exactly that, and it passes both official examples, so it's an easy bug to miss. So the key is size first, and I keep the right end next to it only to check if the entry has expired.

Here's the plan, in three steps. One: sort the query indices by value, so each answer can go back to its slot, and sort the intervals by left end. Two: for each query, push every interval whose left end is at most q, as a pair of size and right end. Three: pop while the top's right end is less than q; whatever is left on top is the answer. Here, I'm using the heap to keep track of every interval that has started, smallest first. One thing worth flagging — I only throw out an expired interval when it reaches the top. Expired ones deeper down never block the top, so they don't hurt. And it's safe, because queries only grow, so an expired interval can never become valid again.
Does that lazy removal cost you anything?

There's a trade-off here. The heap can hold stale entries, so it may grow to all ten to the fifth intervals instead of only the live ones. But each interval is pushed once and popped at most once, so the total work stays the same. And it saves me from deleting from the middle of a heap, which a standard priority queue can't do. Does this approach sound good, or would you rather I think of another way?

Alright, let me code this up. I'll think out loud as I go. The order array holds the query indices, sorted by query value. The heap is a min-heap of pairs, size first, then right end. A pointer i walks the sorted intervals, so each one is pushed exactly once across all queries. The answers start at negative one, so a query with an empty heap just keeps it. One thing worth flagging — the two comparisons. I push while left is at most q, and I pop only while right is strictly less than q. Both ends are included, so an interval that starts or ends exactly at q must still count. And the size needs the plus one: a point interval has size one, not zero.

Let's dry-run the code with an example. Example two: intervals two to three, two to five, one to eight and twenty to twenty-five, with queries two, nineteen, five, twenty-two. Expected two, negative one, four, six. Sorted, the queries go two, five, nineteen, twenty-two. The moment that matters is nineteen. The two entries left, two to five and one to eight, both end before nineteen. I pop both, the heap is empty, and that query stays negative one. Each answer goes back to its original slot, so the output is two, negative one, four, six.

Let's also test with corner cases. If no interval contains the query, the heap ends up empty and the answer stays negative one. A point interval like four to four gets size one, thanks to the plus one. If every interval starts before the first query, the heap holds all ten to the fifth at once, which is fine. And one interval from one to ten million has size ten million, which still fits in an int.

Let me think about complexity here. The time complexity is n log n to sort the intervals, plus q log q to sort the queries. There's a while loop inside the for loop, but the pointer only moves forward and each interval is popped at most once, so all the heap work adds up to n log n. The space complexity is linear, n plus q, for the heap, the order array and the answers. In the worst-case scenario, the heap holds all ten to the fifth intervals. On a random test with ten to the fifth of each, it ran in about twenty-five milliseconds. Oh, one more thing — this needs all the queries up front. If they came one at a time in any order, I couldn't throw away expired intervals, because a later, smaller query might still need them.

Nicely done. Three things stood out. You turned it into an offline problem by sorting the queries and keeping their positions. You showed with a two-interval example why the heap must be keyed by size and not by right end. And you explained why lazy removal is safe: queries only grow, so an expired interval never comes back. Good work.
